claims.text: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi films form a single-phase hexagonal state.
The as-deposited hexagonal phase has substantial atomic-scale chemical disorder with incipient local ordering.
Nanoscale variations in local chemical order control the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Short-range-ordered regions embedded in the disordered hexagonal phase create heterogeneous energy barriers.
These heterogeneous barriers govern the onset and character of the first-order magnetostructural transition.
The relevant nanoscale ordering heterogeneities occur at grain boundaries or within grains.
A controlled mild post-deposition anneal can enhance short-range chemical order without causing large-scale phase separation.
Annealing-induced local atomic rearrangements reduce heterogeneity in the transition-energy barriers.
Reduced barrier disparity facilitates smoother domain nucleation and growth under low applied fields.
Mildly annealed samples will have a broader magnetocaloric transition than the as-deposited baseline.
Mildly annealed samples will have less hysteresis, observable as a smaller magnetic or calorimetric loop area.
The annealed samples will preserve a magnetocaloric entropy-change amplitude comparable to that of the as-deposited samples.
Annealing may shift the magnetostructural transition temperature slightly.
As-deposited films exhibit a sharply defined first-order magnetostructural transition with a large but hysteretic entropy change.
The predictions are limited to non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys in the magnetic-refrigeration compositional window under low-field cycling.
The predicted behavior may fail when annealing is sufficiently aggressive to cause phase separation.
The predicted behavior may not hold at fields significantly above the low-field regime.
Stress relaxation or changes in magnetic anisotropy may also contribute to the annealing response.
Failure of hysteresis reduction or transition broadening despite verified enhancement of short-range order would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
